subject: Georgia
note: Hand-curated research for the first Geographica episode (#73). Every narrated fact cites a source; map geometry is drawn from Natural Earth and is not evidence for any of these claims.

claims.text: Georgia lies in the South Caucasus, a region between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea; Georgia's western coast is on the Black Sea.
claims.note: Georgia borders the Black Sea only; it does not touch the Caspian. Say the region sits between the seas, not that Georgia borders both.

claims.text: Chemical evidence of grape wine was found in pottery from two early Neolithic villages, Gadachrili Gora and Shulaveris Gora, about 50 km south of Tbilisi.
The wine residues date to about 6000–5800 BC, roughly 8,000 years ago.
The 2017 study reported this as the earliest biomolecular (chemical) evidence of grape wine from the Near East, about 600–1,000 years earlier than the previous record from Hajji Firuz Tepe in Iran.
claims.note: Attribute the 'earliest' claim to the 2017 study; don't state it as a timeless fact.

claims.text: The residues came from large clay jars, likely used to ferment, age and store wine.
The traditional Georgian method of winemaking in qvevri (egg-shaped clay vessels) was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2013.

tbilisi.note: Capital of Georgia; the marker places the city, not the dig sites.

dig-sites-approx.note: A point about 50 km south of Tbilisi, marking the reported area of both sites, labelled as approximate. Not surveyed coordinates.
